argument.name: The Convergence Argument: Five Paths to One God
argument.overview:
This is not one of Feser’s own numbered arguments but a synthesis of the whole book, built from the formal statements of chapters 1–5 and the unity section at the start of chapter 6. It has three stages.

**Stage A** restates, in compressed form, the conclusion of each of the five proofs. Each pair of steps compresses a long argument; consult the chapter modules for the full formal statements (50, 38, 29, 36 and 27 steps respectively). Each proof is meant to succeed on its own.

**Stage B** shows that the five conclusions describe one and the same being. It relies on two-way entailments among pure actuality, simplicity, subsistent existence and necessity, plus the argument that none of these can be had by more than one thing.

**Stage C** draws out what follows: a single being with the full set of divine attributes, sustaining and empowering everything else at every moment — which is what classical theism means by God.

> Remember that ‘cumulative’ here does not mean ‘probabilistic’. The case does not add up five weak arguments into one stronger bet; it shows five independent demonstrations arriving at the same place, and it explains *why* they must.

stages.title: Stage A — Five independent routes
stages.gist: Each proof, from its own starting point, establishes a being fitting a distinctive description: purely actual actualizer, absolutely simple One, necessary intellect, subsistent existence itself, necessary being.

stages.title: Stage B — One referent
stages.gist: Pure actuality, simplicity, subsistent existence and necessity entail one another; a necessary intellect is purely actual; and there cannot in principle be two such beings. So the five conclusions name one being.

stages.title: Stage C — The God of classical theism
stages.gist: That one being has every attribute derived by any route, conserves and concurs with all things, and is therefore God — reached by five distinct paths.

steps.text: Change is real, and every change presupposes a thing that changes, whose existence at each moment requires the concurrent actualization of its potential to exist.
steps.why: Chapter 1: change cannot coherently be denied (denying it is itself a change), and change is the actualization of potential. The coffee’s water exists here and now only because its matter’s potential to be water is being actualized, via atoms, via subatomic particles, and so on.

steps.text: So there exists a purely actual actualizer — an Unmoved (indeed unmovable) Mover.
steps.why: Chapter 1: the regress of concurrent actualizers of existence is hierarchical, and a hierarchical series must end in something with underived power that can actualize without being actualized, i.e., something with no potency at all.

steps.text: The things of our experience are composite, and a composite exists at any moment only if its parts are combined at that moment by a cause distinct from it.
steps.why: Chapter 2: the whole depends on the parts being put together; it cannot be the cause of its own composition without vicious circularity. This holds for physical parts and metaphysical ones (form and matter, essence and existence).

steps.text: So there exists an absolutely simple, noncomposite cause — the One.
steps.why: Chapter 2: the regress of composing causes is hierarchical and must have a first member, and any composite first member would need a cause of its own; so the first member has no parts of any kind.

steps.text: Abstract objects — universals, propositions, numbers, possible worlds — are real, are not dependent on the material world or on human (or any contingent) minds, and cannot exist in a Platonic ‘third realm’.
steps.why: Chapter 3: direct arguments for realism, decisive problems for nominalism and conceptualism, the causal inertness and incoherence of Platonic Forms, and the inability of Aristotelian realism alone to ground necessary truths and pure possibilities.

steps.text: So abstract objects exist as ideas in a necessarily existing intellect that grasps their entire interlocking system.
steps.why: Chapter 3: the only remaining home for abstractions is an intellect; contingent intellects cannot ground necessary and eternal truths; and because abstract objects are logically interconnected, one intellect must grasp them all (a ‘conceptually omniscient’ being).

steps.text: In each thing we experience, essence is really distinct from existence, so that each such thing must have existence imparted to it by another at every moment it exists.
steps.why: Chapter 4: we can know essences without knowing existence; things are contingent; and something whose essence is existence could only be one. Nothing can impart existence to itself, and the need for existence to be imparted persists as long as the distinction does — here and now.

steps.text: So there exists a cause whose essence just is existence — subsistent existence itself.
steps.why: Chapter 4: a regress of causes that are themselves essence-existence composites is hierarchical and must terminate in something that need not receive existence because it is existence.

steps.text: The principle of sufficient reason is true, and neither any contingent thing nor any series of contingent things (even an infinite one) can explain why contingent things exist or why any particular contingent thing persists now.
steps.why: Chapter 5: PSR is inductively confirmed and denying it undermines perception, reasoning and explanation; contingency transfers from parts to collection; appeal to further contingent causes merely relocates the problem.

steps.text: So there exists an absolutely necessary being, whose existence is explained by its own nature.
steps.why: Chapter 5: explanation is either by another or by one’s own nature; PSR excludes explanation by nothing; so the regress must end in something necessary.

steps.text: Whatever has parts of any kind is a mixture of actuality and potentiality.
steps.why: Chapter 6 (Unity), drawing on chapter 2: parts only potentially compose a whole until something actually combines them, and this is true even if the whole has always existed.

steps.text: Whatever has any potentiality is thereby composite, having an actual ‘part’ and a potential ‘part’.
steps.why: Chapter 2 (stage 2) and chapter 6: a simple being must be at least partly actual in order to exist and cause, and any added potency would be a second constituent.

steps.text: So something is purely actual if and only if it is absolutely simple: the conclusions of steps 2 and 4 describe the same kind of being.
steps.why: Follows from 11 and 12. This is why chapter 2 concludes that the One and the Unmoved Mover are in fact identical — one reality approached from composition rather than from change.

steps.text: In anything whose essence is distinct from its existence, essence and existence are related as potency to act.
steps.why: Chapter 4 (stage 2): Fido’s essence by itself is only a potential dog; only when existence is imparted is there an actual dog.

steps.text: So something is purely actual if and only if it is subsistent existence itself: the conclusions of steps 2 and 8 describe the same kind of being — and, given 13, so does step 4.
steps.why: From 14: pure actuality leaves no room for an essence that merely potentially exists; and if subsistent existence depended on any actualization it would have derived existence and not be existence itself. A simple being cannot have an essence-existence composition, and subsistent existence can have no parts of any other kind either.

steps.text: To be contingent is to depend for existence on the actualization of some potency, on the combining of parts, or on existence being added to an essence.
steps.why: Chapters 4–6: these are exactly the ways something can fail to exist of itself. Chapter 5 identifies them as the underlying reason why contingent things are contingent.

steps.text: So something is absolutely necessary if and only if it is purely actual, simple and subsistent existence itself: the conclusion of step 10 describes the same kind of being as steps 2, 4 and 8.
steps.why: From 16 in both directions: a purely actual, simple, self-existent being has nothing it depends on; a necessary being can have no potency, parts or distinct essence without becoming dependent (chapter 5, stage 2; chapter 6, Unity).

steps.text: A necessarily existing intellect must be purely actual.
steps.why: Chapter 3 (stage 2): if its existence presupposed the actualization of some potential, it would exist contingently on that actualization — contradicting its necessity.

steps.text: There cannot in principle be more than one being that is purely actual (equivalently: simple, subsistent existence itself, absolutely necessary).
steps.why: Chapters 1, 2, 4 and 6: two such beings would need a differentiating feature — a specific difference, a parcel of matter, a perfection one lacks — and any such feature is a part or a potency, which such a being cannot have.

steps.text: So the purely actual actualizer, the One, the necessary intellect, subsistent existence itself and the necessary being are one and the same being.
steps.why: From 13, 15, 17, 18 and 19: all five descriptions apply to one kind of being, and there can be only one of that kind. Like ‘morning star’ and ‘evening star’, the descriptions differ in sense but share a single referent (chapter 2’s Fregean point).

steps.text: Whatever is in an effect is in its total cause formally, virtually or eminently (the principle of proportionate causality).
steps.why: Chapters 1 and 6: a cause cannot give what it does not in some way have — the $20 in my wallet, in my account, or in my power to print it. Defended against Cottingham’s counterexamples in chapter 6.

steps.text: So this one being contains the forms of all possible things in the way an intellect does, and knows all things: it has intellect and omniscience.
steps.why: From 20 and 21 (chapter 1, stage 2; chapter 6, Omniscience): as the cause of every possible thing, it must contain their forms, but not concretely (it is immaterial), so abstractly, as in a mind. Step 6 reaches the same result directly, and knowledge of contingent truths follows from pure actuality (chapter 3).

steps.text: Being purely actual and simple, this one being is also immutable, eternal (timeless), immaterial, incorporeal, perfect, fully good, omnipotent, uncaused and the cause of everything other than itself.
steps.why: Stage 2 of every chapter: no potency means no change, hence no time and no matter; perfection and goodness are actuality, badness is privation; all power to actualize derives from it; being unique, everything else is composite and depends on it.

steps.text: Nothing other than this being could exist for an instant, or act at all, unless it were conserving that thing in being and concurring with its activity.
steps.why: Chapter 6 (Conservation and concurrence): the causal proofs concern dependence here and now; and by agere sequitur esse, what cannot exist independently cannot act independently. This rules out existential inertia, pantheism, panentheism, occasionalism and deism.

steps.text: For there to exist a single, simple, purely actual, necessary, eternal, immaterial, omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good cause of all other things, which conserves them in being, is just what it is for God to exist.
steps.why: The final premise of each chapter’s formal statement: this is what classical theism — pagan, Jewish, Muslim and Christian — has meant by ‘God’. It is not a stipulation smuggled in; it is the traditional concept.

steps.text: So God exists.
steps.why: From 20, 22–25. And he exists as one God, not five: the proofs are distinct paths to one and the same reality.

steps.text: So the case is robust: to escape it, a critic must refute each of the five demonstrations independently, and the convergence explains why their conclusions interlock rather than being a coincidence.
steps.why: Since steps 1–10 are independent routes and steps 11–20 show why they coincide, defeating one proof leaves four; and the interlocking conclusions show that the divine attributes are facets of one idea (pure actuality, subsistent being) rather than an arbitrary list. This last step is the course’s framing of the book’s cumulative force.

keyTerms.definition: The part of philosophy that investigates what unaided reason, apart from revelation, can know about God’s existence, nature and relation to the world.
keyTerms.example: The five proofs and chapter 6’s derivation of the divine attributes are natural theology; the doctrine of the Trinity is not.

keyTerms.definition: The mainstream conception of God in Western philosophy and religion — God as absolutely simple, immutable, eternal, purely actual, subsistent being itself — defended by Aristotle, Plotinus, Augustine, Maimonides, Avicenna, Aquinas and others.
keyTerms.example: Contrasted with ‘theistic personalism’, which treats God as a very great person within a genus of persons.

keyTerms.definition: Actuality is the way a thing really is; potentiality is a real but unrealized capacity to be otherwise. Change is the actualization of a potential.
keyTerms.example: Hot coffee is actually hot and potentially cold — but not potentially chicken soup.

keyTerms.definition: Any potential that is actualized is actualized by something already actual. It concerns what goes from potential to actual, not ‘everything’.
keyTerms.example: The coffee’s potential coldness cannot make itself actual; the cool air or an ice cube does.

keyTerms.definition: A series in which every member other than the first has its causal power only derivatively, from the one before it; it must have a first member with underived power.
keyTerms.example: Cup held up by desk, desk by floor, floor by foundation; a stone pushed by a stick pushed by a hand.

keyTerms.definition: A series ordered through time in which each member has its own causal power once it exists; Feser grants such a series could, in principle, have no beginning.
keyTerms.example: Grandfather begets father, who begets son — the son is begotten even if the grandfather is long dead.

keyTerms.definition: A cause that is first because its causal power is underived, not because it comes earliest in time.
keyTerms.example: Even an infinitely long paintbrush handle needs a painter; the painter is ‘first’ however long the handle.

keyTerms.definition: A cause with no potentiality whatsoever, which can actualize other things without being actualized itself.
keyTerms.example: The terminus of chapter 1’s argument from the existence of the coffee here and now.

keyTerms.definition: To be composite is to have parts (physical or metaphysical) that must be combined; the One is the absolutely simple, noncomposite first cause of all composites.
keyTerms.example: A chair needs its legs, screws and seat held together; the One has no parts to hold together.

keyTerms.definition: The doctrine that God has no parts of any kind — no matter and form, no genus and difference, no essence distinct from existence, no distinct attributes; his power, intellect and goodness are one reality under different descriptions.
keyTerms.example: ‘God’s power’ and ‘God’s intellect’ differ in sense but have one referent, like ‘morning star’ and ‘evening star’.

keyTerms.definition: Universals, propositions, numbers and possible worlds — objects of thought that are not material and cannot be perceived by the senses.
keyTerms.example: The proposition that snow is white, expressed by both ‘Snow is white’ and ‘Schnee ist weiss’.

keyTerms.definition: Platonic: abstract objects exist in a mind-independent ‘third realm’. Aristotelian: universals exist in things, and as abstract only in minds. Scholastic: Aristotelian realism plus the thesis that abstract objects exist in an infinite divine intellect.
keyTerms.example: The Augustinian proof eliminates the first two and concludes to the third.

keyTerms.definition: A thing’s essence is what it is; its existence is the fact that it is. In everything except God these are really distinct.
keyTerms.example: You can know what a unicorn is without knowing whether any exist.

keyTerms.definition: A real distinction reflects a difference in things themselves; a conceptual one only a difference in how we think or speak. A real distinction need not involve separability.
keyTerms.example: ‘Bachelor’/‘unmarried man’ is merely conceptual; a circle’s radius and circumference are really distinct though inseparable.

keyTerms.definition: Aquinas’ description of a being whose essence just is existence, which therefore need not and could not receive existence from anything.
keyTerms.example: The terminus of chapter 4’s regress of causes imparting existence to Fido here and now.

keyTerms.definition: A contingent thing depends on something outside itself and could fail to exist; a necessary being (in the strictest sense) exists by its own nature and depends on nothing.
keyTerms.example: Stones, trees, universes and multiverses are contingent; only what is purely actual, simple and subsistent existence is necessary in the strict sense.

keyTerms.definition: Everything is intelligible: whatever exists has an explanation of its existence and attributes, either in itself or in something else.
keyTerms.example: Even an unsolved murder has an explanation, including of why it remains unsolved.

keyTerms.definition: A supposed fact with no explanation at all, neither in itself nor in anything else. PSR denies there are any.
keyTerms.example: Mackie and Russell suggested the most fundamental laws of nature are brute facts; Feser argues that would make all explanations resting on them illusory.

keyTerms.definition: Whatever is in an effect must be in its total cause in some way — formally, virtually or eminently.
keyTerms.example: The $20 you receive was in my wallet (formally), my bank account (virtually), or my power to print money (eminently).

keyTerms.definition: ‘Action follows being’: what a thing does reflects and cannot exceed what it is.
keyTerms.example: Stones don’t grow or reproduce because they are not living things; a thing that could not act independently of God could not exist independently of him.

keyTerms.definition: Using a term in senses that are neither identical (univocal) nor unrelated (equivocal) but related; it remains literal. Two kinds: analogy of attribution and analogy of proper proportionality.
keyTerms.example: ‘Good wine’ and ‘good man’; ‘seeing a tree’ and ‘seeing that a theorem is true’.

keyTerms.definition: A ‘change’ in something that consists only in a change in something else related to it, not a real change in the thing itself.
keyTerms.example: Socrates becomes shorter than Plato when Plato grows; God becomes Creator when the world comes to be, with no real change in God.

keyTerms.definition: Inferring that a feature that merely happens to accompany something in our experience belongs to it essentially.
keyTerms.example: ‘Every actualizer we know changes as it acts, so any possible actualizer must change’ — like concluding every possible president must be under seven feet tall.

keyTerms.definition: The absence of a feature a thing should have given its nature; on the classical view, all badness is privation.
keyTerms.example: Blindness is the lack of sight in an eye; a tree’s weak roots are a privation, its lack of wings is not.

keyTerms.definition: The doctrine that nothing could continue to exist for an instant unless God were sustaining it in being; creation is ongoing, not a past event.
keyTerms.example: Answers the ‘existential inertia’ view that things tend to stay in existence on their own.

keyTerms.definition: The view that creatures are real (secondary) causes but can act only with God’s cooperation at every moment — the middle ground between occasionalism and mere conservationism.
keyTerms.example: You and the blue chalk jointly produce a blue square: the chalk makes it blue, you make there be a square.

keyTerms.definition: Recent views that treat God as the unique member of a genus of persons, differing from us only in lacking our limitations, and so deny or weaken divine simplicity.
keyTerms.example: Plantinga’s and Swinburne’s views, as classified by Brian Davies; Feser argues such a ‘god’ would be a superangel needing a cause.

keyTerms.definition: The view that science is the only genuine source of knowledge, so that any worthwhile philosophy must be implicit in science.
keyTerms.example: Alex Rosenberg’s argument from the predictive success of physics; Feser compares it to inferring that only metal exists from the success of metal detectors.

keyTerms.definition: A deduction whose conclusion follows necessarily from premises that are certain and cannot be overturned by further empirical inquiry, as opposed to a probabilistic or best-explanation argument.
keyTerms.example: ‘Change occurs’ is known through experience, but no future experience could overturn it, since that experience would itself be a change.

keyTerms.definition: An event with a supernatural cause that either elevates a nature beyond its own powers or suspends its operation by God’s refraining from conserving or concurring — not a ‘violation’ of natural law.
keyTerms.example: A resurrection adds to nature’s course; the three young men unburnt in the furnace involve a subtraction.

distinctions.name: Linear vs. hierarchical causal series

left.label: Linear (per accidens)
left.desc: Members are ordered through time and each has causal power of its own once it exists; an earlier member can vanish without the later one ceasing to act. Feser grants such a series might have no beginning.

right.label: Hierarchical (per se)
right.desc: Every member other than the first acts only with power borrowed, here and now, from a prior member; remove the source and the whole series stops. Such a series must have an underived first member.

distinctions.whyItMatters: This single distinction disarms three of the commonest objections at once: that the argument assumes a beginning of the universe, that an infinite regress could explain everything, and that Hume showed first causes unnecessary. All four causal proofs run on hierarchical series.

distinctions.name: ‘First’ in time vs. ‘first’ as underived

left.label: Temporally first
left.desc: The earliest member of a sequence — the one at the head of the queue, such as a supposed first moment of the Big Bang.

right.label: Underived (primary)
right.desc: The member whose causal power is its own rather than borrowed, and on which every other member depends for its power at every moment, however many intermediaries there are.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Critics often hear ‘first cause’ as ‘earliest cause’ and reply with beginningless cosmologies. Feser’s first cause is first the way the painter is first relative to an infinitely long brush handle.

distinctions.name: Demonstration vs. probabilistic hypothesis

left.label: Best-explanation / probabilistic reasoning
left.desc: Like design arguments and ‘god of the gaps’ reasoning: a hypothesis judged more likely, simpler or better-fitting than rivals, which could be displaced by a better scientific account.

right.label: Metaphysical demonstration
right.desc: A deduction from premises about what any possible empirical theory presupposes (change, composition, contingency, abstract truths), claiming that no alternative is possible even in principle.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Objections from parsimony, from ‘science will fill the gap’, and from Dawkins’ ‘the designer is more complex’ assume the first model. To refute a demonstration one must show a premise false or an inference invalid.

distinctions.name: Cause vs. sufficient reason

left.label: Cause
left.desc: That which actualizes a potential; it must be distinct from its effect, so nothing can cause itself.

right.label: Sufficient reason (explanation)
right.desc: Whatever makes something intelligible. Every cause is an explanation, but not every explanation is a cause, so something can be self-explanatory without being self-caused.

distinctions.whyItMatters: It explains why PSR says everything has an explanation without making an exception for God, and why the causal principles never say ‘everything has a cause’. Hume’s confusion of the two, per Norris Clarke, launched the ‘What caused God?’ straw man.

distinctions.name: Univocal vs. analogical predication

left.label: Univocal (and its opposite, equivocal)
left.desc: Univocal: exactly the same sense in both uses (‘Fido is a dog’, ‘Rover is a dog’). Equivocal: wholly unrelated senses (‘baseball bat’, ‘bat in the attic’).

right.label: Analogical
right.desc: Related but not identical senses, still literal: by attribution (healthy George, healthy food) or by proper proportionality (seeing a tree, seeing a theorem).

distinctions.whyItMatters: If we spoke of God univocally he would be a creature; if equivocally we would say nothing. Analogy is what lets the proofs give real, positive knowledge of God while preserving his simplicity — and it is what Plantinga’s critique of simplicity overlooks.

distinctions.name: Classical theism vs. theistic personalism

left.label: Theistic personalism (neo-theism)
left.desc: God as the greatest member of a genus of persons, with distinct properties, possibly changeable and in time, differing from us chiefly in degree.

right.label: Classical theism
right.desc: God as absolutely simple, purely actual, immutable, eternal subsistent being itself — personal in having intellect and will, but not ‘a being’ within any genus.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Only the classical God is what the five proofs reach. Feser argues that denying simplicity reduces God to a superangel that would itself need a cause — and that critics who attack ‘God’ as one more item in the universe are attacking theistic personalism, not the God of the proofs.

distinctions.name: Real change vs. Cambridge change

left.label: Real change
left.desc: A thing itself gains or loses some feature, actualizing a potential — Socrates growing hair.

right.label: Cambridge change
right.desc: A new description becomes true of a thing only because something else changed — Socrates becoming shorter than Plato because Plato grew.

distinctions.whyItMatters: It shows how an immutable God can be Creator, can ‘begin’ to be related to a world, and can have contingent truths hold of him (e.g., that he created this world) without any real change or composition in him.

distinctions.name: Platonic realism vs. Scholastic realism

left.label: Platonic realism
left.desc: Abstract objects exist in a third realm outside all minds and matter; things ‘participate’ in them.

right.label: Scholastic realism
right.desc: Abstract objects exist only in things (as instantiated) or in intellects (as abstracted) — and, for necessary truths and pure possibilities, in the necessarily existing divine intellect.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The Augustinian proof’s pivotal move is getting a realist from the first to the second. Many mathematically minded skeptics are already realists; the question becomes where abstract objects can live, and Feser argues only a mind can house them.

illustrations.title: Five trails, one summit
illustrations.body: Picture a mountain approached by five trails from five different valleys: one begins at a river (change), one at a quarry (composition), one at an observatory (mathematical truth), one at a nursery full of living things that might not have existed (essence and existence), and one at a library full of explanations (intelligibility). Hikers on each trail describe the summit differently — ‘the source of all motion’, ‘the undivided peak’, ‘the place where all maps are kept’ — but when they arrive they are standing on the same rock. Use this to explain Stage B of the convergence argument: the descriptions differ in sense, the summit is one.

illustrations.title: The paintbrush with an infinitely long handle
illustrations.body: A brush pushes paint across a canvas only because a hand moves it. Make the handle a mile long, or infinitely long — it still has no power of its own to move. Length is irrelevant; what the series needs is a source with ‘built-in’ power. This is Feser’s key image for a hierarchical series, and why ‘first’ means underived, not earliest. The cup on the desk on the floor on the foundation makes the same point for holding up; the lamp on the chain on the ceiling makes it in the other direction.

illustrations.title: Mirrors, and IOUs
illustrations.body: An infinite row of mirrors, each reflecting the one before, still needs an actual face somewhere outside the series; there cannot be only reflections. An infinite chain of IOUs never amounts to real money unless someone at some point actually pays. Both images (chapters 1, 4 and 7) show why an infinite hierarchical regress explains nothing: every member has only what it received.

illustrations.title: Leibniz’s endlessly copied geometry book
illustrations.body: Suppose a geometry textbook was copied from an earlier copy, that one from another, and so on forever. Each copy has an immediate cause, yet we still have no answer to why the series contains geometry rather than Shakespeare or a car manual, or why the series exists at all. Chapters 5 and 7 use this to show that ‘each member is explained by the previous one’ does not explain everything — and that it is the critic who commits the fallacy of composition by thinking it does.

illustrations.title: Red Lego blocks and heavy stones
illustrations.body: If every stone in a pile weighs under an ounce, the pile need not; but if every Lego block is red, whatever you build from them is red. Whether part-to-whole reasoning works depends on the property. Contingency behaves like color: a collection of contingent things is, if anything, more contingent — ‘doubly contingent’ — than its members. Use it whenever someone says ‘fallacy of composition!’

illustrations.title: Morning star, evening star
illustrations.body: Ancient astronomers named ‘the morning star’ and ‘the evening star’ separately before learning both were Venus. The expressions differ in sense but share a referent. Feser uses Frege’s distinction to explain how God’s omnipotence, intellect and goodness can be one reality in a simple being — and the same idea explains how five proofs with five different conclusions can name one God.

illustrations.title: Three ways to have $20
illustrations.body: I can give you $20 because I have a bill in my wallet (the effect is in the cause formally), because I have $20 in my account (virtually), or because I can have genuine bills printed (eminently). The principle of proportionate causality says an effect must be in its total cause in one of these ways. It is how Stage 2 infers intellect: the cause of every possible thing must contain their forms — not as a cat contains catness, but as a mind contains ideas.

illustrations.title: The author and the story
illustrations.body: An author can conceive a whole story in one flash of insight — beginning, middle and end — while within the story events unfold in order. The author knows every event not by observing it but by knowing his own creative plan. And a character who plots a murder does so freely even though the author wrote it; the author is not a hypnotist inside the story. Chapter 6 uses this to illuminate eternity, omniscience, and the compatibility of divine causality with human freedom.

illustrations.title: The metal detector and the drunk under the lamppost
illustrations.body: A metal detector’s flawless record at finding coins does not show that only metal exists; a drunk who searches for his keys only under the streetlight, because that is where he can see, has no evidence they are nowhere else. Physics is spectacularly successful precisely because it restricts itself to what can be mathematically modelled; its silence about causation, purpose or the intrinsic nature of matter is an artifact of its method, not a discovery. Chapters 1 and 7 deploy these images against Russell, quantum objections and scientism.

illustrations.title: White light and the prism
illustrations.body: All the colors are contained, in a unified way, in white light before a prism separates them. Similarly, all the limited ways of being actual — being a stone, a tree, a dog — are contained in unlimited actuality, and to know pure actuality perfectly would be to know every way it could be limited. Chapter 6 offers this (with the image of cookie dough and cutters) as a way to think about how God knows all things without composition in his knowledge — while warning that God is not a material stuff that creatures are made of.

comparison.startingPoint: Change is real — potentials are actualized (the coffee cools); and the things that change exist here and now only by the concurrent actualization of their potential to exist.
comparison.keyPrinciple: The principle of causality — no potential actualizes itself; plus the thesis that a hierarchical series of actualizers must have an underived first member.
comparison.conclusion: A purely actual actualizer (Unmoved, indeed unmovable, Mover), which Stage 2 shows is one, immutable, eternal, immaterial, perfect, good, omnipotent, intelligent and omniscient.
comparison.keyDistinction: Actuality vs. potentiality; linear (per accidens) vs. hierarchical (per se) causal series.
comparison.bestFor: Science-minded listeners; people who assume the argument is about the Big Bang; anyone who likes concrete, everyday examples and step-by-step causal reasoning.
comparison.mostCommonObjection: ‘If everything has a cause, what caused God?’ — or ‘physics (inertia, quantum mechanics, relativity) shows change can occur without a cause.’
comparison.quickReply: The principle concerns what goes from potential to actual, not ‘everything’; what is purely actual has nothing to be actualized. And physics abstracts from causation by method — absence from the equations is not absence from reality; its own evidence rests on changing experiences.

comparison.startingPoint: The things of our experience are composite — made of parts (legs and screws, organs and cells, form and matter, essence and existence) that must be combined at every moment for the whole to exist.
comparison.keyPrinciple: Whatever is composite requires a concurrent cause of the combination of its parts; nothing can compose itself, and the regress of composers is hierarchical.
comparison.conclusion: An absolutely simple, noncomposite first cause — the One — which is unique, immutable, eternal, a mind, purely actual, and identical with the Unmoved Mover.
comparison.keyDistinction: Composite vs. absolutely simple; temporal vs. atemporal (moment-to-moment) dependence of a whole on its parts.
comparison.bestFor: Engineers, builders and systems thinkers who find ‘what holds this together right now?’ natural; also ideal for teaching divine simplicity to believers.
comparison.mostCommonObjection: ‘Maybe a thing’s parts are unified by one of its parts, or the unity is just a brute fact, or laws of nature explain it.’
comparison.quickReply: A unifying part is one more item needing to be unified (regress); a brute fact is not an alternative explanation but no explanation — and one has been offered; laws plus the things they govern form yet another composite.

comparison.startingPoint: Universals, propositions, numbers and possible worlds are real and are not dependent on the material world or on human minds (2 + 2 = 4 would be true if no humans existed).
comparison.keyPrinciple: Abstract objects can exist only in things or in intellects (there is no Platonic third realm); necessary, eternal, interlocking truths require a necessary, eternal intellect that grasps them all.
comparison.conclusion: A necessarily existing, conceptually omniscient divine intellect — which, being purely actual, is unique, fully omniscient, omnipotent, good, immutable, immaterial and eternal.
comparison.keyDistinction: Realism vs. nominalism and conceptualism; Platonic vs. Aristotelian vs. Scholastic realism.
comparison.bestFor: Mathematicians, logicians, programmers and Platonist-leaning skeptics who already believe in objective, necessary truths.
comparison.mostCommonObjection: ‘Why not simple Platonism — abstract objects existing necessarily in no mind at all?’
comparison.quickReply: Third-realm objects would be causally inert, so they could neither explain why things instantiate them nor be known by us; and a Form would have to be both universal and a particular (animality itself neither rational nor nonrational). Only an intellect can house what is abstract — and only a necessary one can ground necessary truths.

comparison.startingPoint: In each thing we experience, essence (what it is) is really distinct from existence (that it is) — we can know what a lion or unicorn is without knowing whether it exists.
comparison.keyPrinciple: Nothing whose essence is distinct from its existence can give itself existence; it must receive existence from another at every moment, and the regress of such causes is hierarchical.
comparison.conclusion: A cause whose essence just is existence — subsistent existence itself — which is unique, necessary, uncaused, purely actual, the cause of all else, and has all the divine attributes.
comparison.keyDistinction: Essence vs. existence; real vs. merely conceptual distinction (real need not mean separable).
comparison.bestFor: The metaphysically curious, philosophy students, and anyone who asks why anything exists rather than not; people comfortable with abstract reasoning.
comparison.mostCommonObjection: ‘The distinction is merely conceptual (like aspirin and acetylsalicylic acid), or existence is just the logical quantifier’ (Kenny).
comparison.quickReply: A complete grasp of aspirin reveals it is acetylsalicylic acid, but no complete grasp of a lion’s essence reveals its existence; contingency and plurality confirm the real distinction. Kenny assumes real distinction means separability and that quantifier-existence captures everything — both beg the question.

comparison.startingPoint: The principle of sufficient reason: everything has an explanation, either in its own nature or in something else.
comparison.keyPrinciple: Neither a contingent thing nor any series of contingent things (even infinite) can explain why contingent things exist or why any one persists now; only something necessary can end the regress.
comparison.conclusion: An absolutely necessary being, explained by its own nature, which must be purely actual, simple and subsistent existence itself — hence the same God reached by the other proofs.
comparison.keyDistinction: Contingent vs. necessary; cause vs. sufficient reason (self-explanatory is not self-caused).
comparison.bestFor: Lovers of explanation and science, people who ask ‘why is there something rather than nothing?’, and debate settings where the Leibniz–Clarke argument is already familiar.
comparison.mostCommonObjection: ‘PSR is false: the universe or the fundamental laws may simply be brute facts.’
comparison.quickReply: Denying PSR undercuts trust in perception and in our own reasoning, including the reasoning against PSR; brute-fact foundations make every explanation built on them illusory (a book on a shelf that floats for no reason); and there is no principled line for where explanation may stop (Della Rocca).
